title: Stephanie Ahn’s Seven-Year Road to ‘Bedford Park’: ‘You Never Know What Can Make Your Film Better’
description: After winning the U.S. Dramatic Special Jury Award for Debut Feature at Sundance this year, “Bedford Park” has its international premiere at the Tor
body:
After winning the U.S. Dramatic Special Jury Award for Debut Feature at Sundance this year, “Bedford Park” has its international premiere at the Toronto Film Festival, ahead of a U.S. theatrical release by Sony Pictures Classics.

	Speaking with Variety, director Stephanie Ahn and lead actors Moon Choi (“Anarchist From Colony”) and Son Sukku (“Sense8,” “My Liberation Notes”) discussed the surprising journey of bringing Ahn’s semi-autobiographical script to cinemas.
	

	“The movie is about my experience as a Korean American,” says Ahn. “It’s about the pull I’ve always felt towards my passion while being cemented in family and loyalty. It’s about the experience of having love expressed in a very different way in my Korean home and outside of home, in the United States.”


	This tension is embodied by Audrey, a physical therapist with a repressed fighting spirit and slightly kinky sexual encounters. When she meets Eli, a Korean American adoptee, in not-so-ideal circumstances, their relationship blossoms into a romance that redefines them. The story unfolds in the New Jersey suburbs, where Audrey goes back to live with her parents.

	“I auditioned for Audrey seven years ago,” remembers Moon Choi. “It’s rare but Stephanie arranged to send me the whole script ahead of the audition. I read it in one sitting.” This project has been the longest the actress has ever waited to film, as COVID, Hollywood strikes and lack of funding kept threatening production. “I grew old with Audrey,” adds Choi. “I was 31 when I was cast and filmed at 37. It changed my understanding of many scenes.”
	

	Throughout, the script remained the project’s fixed point. It changed considerably over the years, shifting from a family drama into a love story. “I didn’t want a traditional love story. I wanted to make the feeling of them getting together feel inevitable — but not predictable,” says Ahn.

	To achieve this idea, the movie constantly subverts expectations. It often brings the characters together in the same physical space, while their minds are adrift. This tension culminates in an emotional scene where Audrey and Eli are in the car, listening to the “Rocky” soundtrack. An ex-wrestler, Eli dances to the theme while Audrey smiles at his corny enthusiasm, before she truly listens and the music bring her to tears.

	“We did eight or 10 takes because I wanted a single shot, but something wasn’t gelling with the first five or six takes,” says Ahn. “Originally, the scene ended with Eli saying something like ‘Everyone thinks it’s about boxing, but really, it’s a love story’ about ‘Rocky,‘ when I realized — it’s that line. Let’s take it out and not have an end goal. Let’s just have you guys go wherever you’re going when the song plays. And they nailed it.”

	With the movie being all about the characters’ relationships, Ahn needed a powerful chemistry. But, while she cast Moon Choi early on, finding Eli proved to be a challenge. His part was originally written for a Caucasian American actor.

	“When I was growing up, the current fascination with Korean culture was nonexistent,” says Ahn. “It’s still an anomaly to me that it’s such a big part of pop culture now. Maybe a part of me was still in that antiquated way of thinking that an American white person would bring more interest.”

	A friend and colleague of Moon Choi, Son Sukku, was suggested to Ahn by the actress. And, ironically, it is his superstar fame in Korea that finally unlocked funding for the movie from Hyundai. “Bedford Park” marks their fifth collaboration.

	“I think my 15-year old friendship with Moon did help to shape the unique relationship that they show in the movie,” notes Son Sukku when asked about having a role rewritten for him. “But I don’t think much has changed from the original character other than his ethnicity.” The actor also believes his ease to connect with self-hate, anger and a longing to connect with people when acting might have naturally made Eli less aggressive and careless than he imagined him before shooting.
	

	“Thank God Sukku was interested in the role, and not just because we ultimately got funding one or two years after we cast him, but also because the character was so much richer after that,” says Ahn. “It’s funny, looking back I was so reluctant to the idea.” The director met the actor convinced she was going to say no, but she immediately saw the character in him. “You never know what can make your film better,” continues Ahn.

	As an editor, Ahn knew to kill her darlings from experience on movies like “Winter’s Bone” (2010) and “My Old Lady” (2014), which brought her a unique advantage. “I really trusted the script by the time we were shooting and I can’t help but think like an editor,” she says. “While filming, I’ve kind of already constructed the edits in my head. Some people noted there are a lot of short scenes in the movie – which is probably the result of my work as an editor. The story isn’t told by a single scene but by the relationship between scenes for me.”

	This structure allows the movie to touch upon many themes, like the kindness that bonds the leads, the intertwined love and violence present in family relationships, the messy journey to figure out who you are, without letting them cannibalize each other. Driving its core message home: “In the end, this movie is a love story of oneself,” says Choi.

	“It’s the most poignant love story,” adds Ahn.

schema.headline: Stephanie Ahn’s Seven-Year Road to ‘Bedford Park’: ‘You Never Know What Can Make Your Film Better’

title: ‘Like ‘Amores Perros,’ I Hope My Film Will Also Transcend Time in Some Way,’ Says Gael García Bernal of His Third Directorial Outing, ‘Hombre al Agua’
description: Gael García Bernal is best known for his breakout roles in two of Mexico’s most consequential films, “Amores Perros” (2000) and “Y Tu Mama Tambien”
body:
Gael García Bernal is best known for his breakout roles in two of Mexico’s most consequential films, “Amores Perros” (2000) and “Y Tu Mama Tambien” (2001) but he’s also been directing these past years. Proof of his cachet is having his third feature, “Hombre al agua” world premiere at the Venice Biennale and have its North American premiere at Toronto (TIFF).

	The theme of class runs through “Hombre al agua,” as in his first two directorial outings, “Déficit” (2007) and “Chicuarotes” (2019). While “Déficit” exposed underlying class tensions at a party a wealthy teen throws to impress people, “Chicuarotes” centers on two working class teens trying to better their lives.
	

	“I think class is undoubtedly a theme I’m drawn to, partly because the struggle has not been resolved. At the same time, class has been changing rapidly, with circumstances and public attention shifting considerably since I started working in cinema. So, it felt important to explore it, but also to question where we are we now and where we are heading,” he told Variety.


	In “Hombre al agua,” García Bernal plays Camilo, a Cuban lifeguard who saves Abel, a Mexican businessman, from drowning. Grateful, Abel brings him to Mexico to work as his right-hand man and introduces him to his daughter, Juana, whom Camilo later marries. But he gradually realizes that his new life is part of a carefully orchestrated plan. As questions emerge about Abel’s motives, Camilo begins to piece together what is really happening and decides to take control of his future.
	

	As the title suggests, roughly translated to “man overboard,” Camilo is adrift as his marriage falls apart and he tries to move beyond the lie he’s been living.

	“I also wanted to explore the crisis of masculinity, the roles of men and women within a couple, and the experience of separation. I wanted to do all of this through comedy, with a kind of meta-cinematic playfulness, while also looking at the political landscape in Latin America today: where we are, what is happening and where we are going,” he said.

	Reflecting on the impact of “Amores Perros,” he mused: “When it came out, it became something extraordinary and transcended time. Twenty-five years later, we’re still celebrating it.”

	“I hope my film will also transcend time in some way, but that’s something we can never know. Only time will tell. I do hope it says something, because I think it is very relevant to the world we’re living in right now.”

	ENDS

	“It’s amazing how a film can affect people’s lives – not only the people who made it, but also those who watched it. That’s the wonder of cinema. There’s always a strange alchemy to it. So, I’m very aware, making ‘Hombre al agua,’ of how grateful I am to have this opportunity to make the film, to give it our best and to enjoy the process.”Reflecting on all the great directors he’s worked with and the invaluable lessons he learned from them, he said: “From the first two directors I worked with, Alejandro González Iñárritu and Alfonso Cuarón, I learned the value of relentless effort and rigor and of making the most of every opportunity—always pushing to find that extra thing. I also learned from their complete involvement in their films, while understanding how to manage the frustration and disappointment that can come with that level of commitment.”He also looks up to Walter Salles who directed him in the seminal “The Motorcycle Diaries.” “He taught me about friendship and the way he approaches work—with generosity, joy and a huge sense of camaraderie.”“From Michel Gondry [“The Science of Sleep”], I learned that everything has to be worked out in front of the camera, like a play: instead of discussing it, let’s try it. And from Pablo Larraín [“No,” “Neruda,” “Ema”],” a kind of audacity – let’s just go for it, let’s try it, let’s break it.”He started writing “Hombre al Agua” eight or nine years ago, enlisting Argentine playwright Mariano Pensotti to co-write it with him.“The film isn’t linear, so I needed that support—the back-and-forth of ideas. He helped me put everything together, shape the structure and begin building the whole world of the film.”His Latin American cast includes Esmeralda Pimentel (“Almost Paradise”), Debóra Nascimento, Natalia Oreiro and Jorge Salinas (“Amores Perros”).It was shot mainly in the Mexican state of Yucatán, including locations near Mérida and a beach at Sisal, as well as in Mexico City. They also spent three days shooting in Havana in December.“Cuba has its usual logistical challenges, but we had a very light schedule there, so it was quite easy and enjoyable. Havana was also important because it was the only urban setting we wanted to show in the film,” he said.Securing financing was probably the trickiest challenge. Every time he tried to cast a Cuban actor to play Camilo, interest from investors would drop. In the end, the company he founded with Diego Luna, La Corriente del Golfo, produced it along with Cárcava Cine (“The Untamed”) and Stacy Perskie’s Redrum (“Spectre,” “Bardo”).“Apparently, everything now has to be thoroughly and mathematically proven. But that’s impossible with film, because the nature of filmmaking is exploration. To paraphrase Werner Herzog, ‘if you want something completely factual, read a phone book.’ It’s very difficult today to convince companies to take a chance on an adventure, especially with original films that aren’t based on established IP. The film may look expensive, but fortunately we made it with very little money and we’re very happy with the result.”

	Paris-based The Pool Films handles international sales. 



	

					Esmeralda Pimental and Natalia Oreiro with Gael García Bernal. Courtesy of La Corriente del Golfo

schema.headline: ‘Like ‘Amores Perros,’ I Hope My Film Will Also Transcend Time in Some Way,’ Says Gael García Bernal of His Third Directorial Outing, ‘Hombre al Agua’

title: Jimmy Kimmel in Talks to Renew Late-Night Show at ABC
description: Jimmy Kimmel and Disney‘s ABC have entered into negotiations about keeping the host in late-night after the new TV season, a process that might ordi
body:
Jimmy Kimmel and Disney‘s ABC have entered into negotiations about keeping the host in late-night after the new TV season, a process that might ordinarily be the most normal of business practices, but in the current climate is exceedingly fraught.

	Kimmel and executives at the Disney network are having talks about whether he might continue to host “Jimmy Kimmel Live” after the 2026-2027 season, according to a person familiar with the matter. Disney declined to make executives available for comment, and a representative for Kimmel declined to comment as well. James Dixon, the agent who represents Kimmel as well as other late-night notables including Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert, could not be reached for immediate comment.
	

	Kimmel in 2025 moved from a more typical three-year contact to a one-year deal, a sign of not only his long tenure in the role but also the foundering economics of late-night TV, which has ceded not only many of the younger viewers that once flocked to the daypart, but a significant percentage of the ad dollars that followed them. At the same time, shows like “Jimmy Kimmel Live” continue to be part of popular culture, and Kimmel has played a key figure as many of the programs waded more directly into political humor and anti-Trump stances.


	A single-year contract would give both host and broadcaster more flexibility to change plans if the business of wee-hours TV grew more challenged.

	Puck previously reported that Kimmel and the Disney TV network had entered into renewal talks.

	The talks are likely to touch upon some difficult realities. Spending on late night television shows hit $209 million in 2025, according to data from Guideline, a tracker of ad expenditures, down from $519.7 million in 2017. Ad spending on “Jimmy Kimmel Live” totaled $51.1 million in 2024, accounting for 21% of all late night spend, according to the firm — a percentage that is well behind that for NBC’s “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon” and CBS’ now defunct “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert.”
	

	And yet, Kimmel’s program has gotten a ratings boost since CBS removed Colbert’s show from its schedule in May. That means “Jimmy Kimmel Live” can likely charge more money for the new group it reaches. At the same time, Kimmel’s monologues that rail against President Trump, and decisions to poke the bear by putting Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico of Texas on a YouTube stream have invited increased scrutiny from the White House and the Federal Communications Commission.

	Disney is at present enmeshed in legal wrangling with the FCC, alleging that the regulator had encroached on ABC’s First Amendment rights by moving to punish it for its news coverage and programming decisions. The FCC ordered Disney to file for renewals for ABC’s eight owned-and-operated stations years ahead of schedule. In filings, Disney has said its applications were made “under protest in response to an unlawful, arbitrary, and unconstitutional order.” “The View,” which has thrived in recent years with discussion of politics, has also found itself in the administration’s cross-hairs.

	More to come…

schema.headline: Jimmy Kimmel in Talks to Renew Late-Night Show at ABC

title: ‘Sheriff Country’ Sets Backdoor Pilot for Medical Spinoff Starring ‘Schitt’s Creek’ Actor Noah Reid
description: Noah Reid will guest star in two upcoming episodes of “Sheriff Country,” which will function as a backdoor pilot for a spinoff set in the same unive
body:
Noah Reid will guest star in two upcoming episodes of “Sheriff Country,” which will function as a backdoor pilot for a spinoff set in the same universe.

	Pending a decision from CBS, Reid would potentially be a series regular on a medical drama set in the same universe as “Sheriff Country” and “Fire Country.” If greenlit, the series will follow a team of healthcare professionals in Edgewater, Calif.

	Reid will play Dr. Hudson “Hud” Henshaw, the chief of emergency medicine at Edgewater Memorial Hospital aka “Edge Med.” The official character description reads, “Charming and quick-witted, but rough-around-the-edges, Hud was born and raised in the outlaw hinterland known as Deadwater. He is the proud son of convicted felons, yet refused to take the family’s drug money to pay for medical school. He is a passionate doctor who embodies his oath to ‘first do no harm,’ yet is not one to shy away from a good bar fight. A man deeply committed to the community he grew up in, he is a restless soul all the same.”
	

	More to come…

schema.headline: ‘Sheriff Country’ Sets Backdoor Pilot for Medical Spinoff Starring ‘Schitt’s Creek’ Actor Noah Reid

title: ‘Point Break’ TV Series Greenlit at AMC, Canal+
description:
The “Point Break” followup series has officially been ordered at AMC and AMC+, Variety has learned. 

	The modern update of the beloved 1991 action
body:
The “Point Break” followup series has officially been ordered at AMC and AMC+, Variety has learned. 

	The modern update of the beloved 1991 action film was first reported to be in the works at the network back in December 2025. As reported at the time, the show hails from lead studio Alcon Television Group as well as AMC Studios and StudioCanal, who will co-produce. StudioCanal, a Canal+ company, will handle international sales and worldwide distribution outside the U.S. and Canada. 
	

	The first season of the series will consist of eight episodes. Production is slated to begin in early 2027. 


	The logline for the series states, “More than three decades after the events of the original ‘Point Break’ film, a new heist crew inspired by the Ex-Presidents has emerged and the FBI must rely on a mysterious ex-pro surfer with a checkered past to infiltrate them.” 

	Dave Kalstein and Christopher C. Rogers serve as co-showrunners and executive producers on the series. Alcon co-founders and co-CEOs Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson executive produce, as do Alcon Television Group head Ben Roberts and Julia Cohen. M-K Kennedy, Paul Gilbert and Daniel Gratton are overseeing the project for StudioCanal. Steven Johnson, Diego Piasek, and Gene Hong will serve as co-executive producers, with Emily Yoshida and Ben Cook as supervising producers.

	“Start with one of the most entertaining and unforgettable action films ever made, add a powerhouse creative team and producing partners, massive fan interest that has been clear from the moment we announced the series was in development and you get a greenlight we could not be more excited about,” said Dan McDermott, chief content officer of AMC Global Media and president of AMC Studios. “Dave Kalstein and Chris Rogers have created a story and characters that honor the legacy of the film and will bring a new generation of Ex-Presidents to the world.”
	

	The original “Point Break” starred Keanu Reeves as rookie FBI agent Johnny Utah and Patrick Swayze as Bohdi, surf king and leader of the Ex-Presidents. Lori Petty and Gary Busey also starred. The film has become a cult classic in the years since its release. 

	“’Point Break’ was the movie that rocked our worlds forever,” Kalstein and Rogers said in a joint statement. “It was this wild cinematic sermon on friendship, outlaws, and spirituality that struck our souls. As we got older, we realized it hit millions of people the same way. ‘Point Break’ is more than just a movie—it’s a way of looking at the world. We are so honored to be carrying this legacy forward with Alcon, AMC, and StudioCanal. We’re putting together a series that will inspire audiences everywhere to seek The Ultimate.”

	This will not be the first attempt to bring “Point Break” into the 21st century. A remake of the film starring Luke Bracey as Johnny and Édgar Ramírez as Bohdi was released in 2015. It performed moderately well at the box office but was roundly rejected by critics upon its debut. 

	“We’re excited to see ‘Point Break’ move into production with AMC,” said Johnson and Kosove. “Dave and Chris have a strong vision for the series and a clear understanding of what makes this world so compelling. We’re looking forward to working closely with AMC and the creative team to bring this series to audiences.” 

	This marks the latest new series order at AMC recently. The network is also currently at work on the NASCAR series “Thunder Road” starring Dennis Quaid. AMC is also preparing to launch the final season of “The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon,” which will debut in 2027, and recently aired the Silicon Valley drama “The Audacity.” 

	“The opportunity to ride this legendary wave with AMC Studios and Alcon Television Group, bringing this globally beloved IP to Canal+ subscribers and audiences around the world was beyond compelling,” said Kennedy, the managing director for StudioCanal Worldwide Television. “We can’t wait to get started!”

schema.headline: ‘Point Break’ TV Series Greenlit at AMC, Canal+

title: Maria Bartiromo Says ‘More to Come’ in First Comments After Shock Fox News Exit: ‘I Am So Grateful for the Outpouring of Love’
description:
Maria Bartiromo shared her first public comments since her sudden exit from Fox News and Fox Business last week.

	In a post on social media, Bartir
body:
Maria Bartiromo shared her first public comments since her sudden exit from Fox News and Fox Business last week.

	In a post on social media, Bartiromo thanked “all friends & followers” for their support, and shared a photo of a rainbow breaking through clouds. She also teased that there will be “more to come” in her story.

	“Thank you to all friends & followers for your amazing words I am so grateful for the outpouring of love on SM & texts,” Baritroomo wrote in a post Thursday on X. “I love you all. here’s a great shot of the 🌈 breaking through, I snapped the other day. More to come”
	

	Bartiromo, who had been with Fox News and Fox Business for more than 12 years, was originally hired as a business anchor. In recent years, she has become increasingly enamored of Trump and has promoted various MAGA conspiracy theories. Bartiromo was the first Fox anchor to promote false claims about the 2020 presidential election; she was among Fox News staffers including Sean Hannity and Jeanine Pirro who were named in a $1.6 billion defamation lawsuit filed by voting technology company Dominion Voting Systems against Fox News in 2021. Fox ultimately settled the matter, paying Dominion $787.5 million.

	SEE ALSO: Maria Bartiromo vs. Fox News: Anchor’s Pivot Between MAGA Politics and Wall Street Likely Spurred Fallout

	On Sept. 3, Fox News said it parted ways with Bartiromo, who joined as an anchor at both Fox Business Network and Fox News Channel in 2013. “We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 ½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter,” the company said in a statement.
	

	The following day, Bartiromo‘s attorney, Bryan Freedman, said that she had not been fired by Fox and suggested she was ready to take legal action against the company. “The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false,” Freedman said.

	Citing a source familiar with the situation, Variety reported that Fox News believes Bartiromo shared with the White House a directive from network bosses cautioning staffers against supporting outlandish claims made by Trump. Bartiromo had wanted to pursue a story about Trump’s claims in a July 16 speech, in which he alleged China had illegally accessed millions of voter files to try to manipulate U.S. elections in 2018 and 2020, media industry newsletter Status reported.

	Meanwhile, President Donald Trump shared his surprise about Fox taking Bartiromo off the air. “I can’t believe Maria Bartiromo is no longer going to have her great show(s) on FoxNews/Business,” Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account. “Three different shows, always number one. Maria is a total professional, and a true warrior. Her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy. God bless you, Maria!”

Thank you to all friends & followers for your amazing words I am so grateful for the outpouring of love on SM & texts. I love you all. here's a great shot of the 🌈 breaking through, I snapped the other day. More to come pic.twitter.com/toHBSsZok7— Maria Bartiromo (@MariaBartiromo) September 10, 2026

schema.headline: Maria Bartiromo Says ‘More to Come’ in First Comments After Shock Fox News Exit: ‘I Am So Grateful for the Outpouring of Love’

title: ‘Long Day’s Journey Into Night’ Film With Jessica Lange and Ed Harris Lands Quiver Distribution Deal
description: The feature film adaptation of Eugene O’Neill’s Pulitzer-winning play “Long Day’s Journey Into Night” has been acquired by Quiver Distribution, sta
body:
The feature film adaptation of Eugene O’Neill’s Pulitzer-winning play “Long Day’s Journey Into Night” has been acquired by Quiver Distribution, starring Jessica Lange and Ed Harris. 

	Lange will reprise her Tony-winning role as Mary Tyrone, starring alongside Harris as her husband, James. Releasing in select theaters Sept. 25, the film will also be screened at Film at Lincoln Center on Monday. 


	“To translate and adapt what is arguably America’s greatest play to the screen demands, above all, a remarkable cast,” director Jonathan Kent told Variety. “Working with Ed Harris and the brilliant Jessica Lange —who I directed on Broadway in the same role — was an exhilarating experience. They are both as supremely accomplished on screen as they are on stage. The core of the film inevitably has to lie with the portrait of the tragic Tyrone family — these four actors, I believe, achieve this magnificently.”
	

	Also starring in “Long Day’s Journey Into Night” are Ben Foster as the alcoholic eldest son, Jamie, and Colin Morgan as the optimistically poetic younger son, Edmund, who is based on O’Neill. The author’s autobiographical play follows the Tyrone family as they work through their personal traumas while navigating a balance of love and resentment they hold toward each other. 

	“We are thrilled to bring director Jonathan Kent’s remarkable feature debut to U.S. audiences,” said Berry Meyerowitz and Jeff Sackman, the co-presidents of Quiver Distribution. “Kent has brought together a powerhouse cast, led by the incredible Jessica Lange to tell O’Neill’s story. Jessica is nothing short of mesmerizing, giving what may be the defining performance of her illustrious career across stage and screen.”
	

	“Long Day’s Journey Into Night” is produced by Gabrielle Tana, Bill Kenwright and Gleb Fetisov and Redmond Morris. David Lindsay-Abaire adapted the play for screen.

schema.headline: ‘Long Day’s Journey Into Night’ Film With Jessica Lange and Ed Harris Lands Quiver Distribution Deal

title: ‘Dolly Parton International Airport’ Moves Closer to Becoming a Reality, as Nashville Airport Board Votes Unanimously for Name Change
description: The idea of renaming Nashville’s airport for Dolly Parton was not just an easily forgotten pipe dream that popped up in the days following the super
body:
The idea of renaming Nashville’s airport for Dolly Parton was not just an easily forgotten pipe dream that popped up in the days following the superstar’s death in August. The proposal moved a big step closer to reality Friday, as the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority voted 6-0 to officially start the process of changing the airport’s name in her honor.

	What exactly the new name would be has not been settled — although Dolly Parton International Airport appears to be the obvious de facto possibility — and there are further approvals yet to come. But Nashville locals seem more convinced than ever, in the wake of the unanimous vote and previous support from top governmental officials, that this is all but a done deal.
	

	“While a final name has not yet been determined,” the Authority said in an announcement following the vote, “we are working closely with the appropriate parties to thoughtfully determine how Dolly Parton’s name and legacy will be incorporated. This vote represents the first step in a multifaceted process. In the coming months, we anticipate having more definitive plans to share regarding the next steps and implementation. We are grateful for the tremendous support and enthusiasm from our community and Dolly’s fans around the world. We look forward to sharing additional details as plans are finalized.”


	The idea had come up even before the death of Parton (pictured above at London’s Heathrow Airport in 1977). In an interview with the Tennessean newspaper in January 2025, amid development of her forthcoming Broadway musical, the star was asked about the prospect. She treated it lightly at the time. “”I think that’s probably more of a joke than anything,” she said. “I mean, it does sound like a lot of fun to say: ‘Your flight is departin’ from Nashville’s D. Parton.'”
	

	Now, it’s seeming likely we can count on hearing that jocular catchphrase employed as an actual slogan for decades to come.

	Support for the honor has come from a lot of corners — including the general public’s, with more than 175,000 people having signed a Change.org petition supporting a name change.

	Perhaps more importantly for its chances of success, both Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell had come out in favor of a name change. In late August, Lee said in a statement, “From her rural mountain home in East Tennessee to global stages, Dolly carried the Volunteer Spirit with her. At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith and kindness.”

	Her estate has not publicly issued any comment on whether it supports a name change. Parton had not been willing to go along with just any governmental honor, as was proven in 2021 when she personally put a kabosh on a state legislator’s proposal to have a statue of the performer put up in front of the Tennessee capitol. But, of course, an airport carries fewer negative connotations than Tennessee’s eternally controversial state legislature.

	Considerable expense would go into rebranding the entire airport and its facilities. One thing that would remain is the BNA three-letter designation, which would be unaffected by an official name change.

schema.headline: ‘Dolly Parton International Airport’ Moves Closer to Becoming a Reality, as Nashville Airport Board Votes Unanimously for Name Change

title: ‘Hombre al Agua’ Review: Gael García Bernal Directs and Stars in a Sputtering, Screwball-y Dramedy About One Man’s Identity Crisis
description: Sifting through Gael García Bernal’s recent roles — from the namesake conquistador of Lav Diaz’s “Magellan,” the grieving wife-guy in Piero Messina’
body:
Sifting through Gael García Bernal’s recent roles — from the namesake conquistador of Lav Diaz’s “Magellan,” the grieving wife-guy in Piero Messina’s droopy sci-fi “Another End,” and the fast-aging family man of M. Night Shyamalan’s “Old” — won’t give you much insight on “Hombre al Agua,” which translates as “man overboard.” Except that unlike those international productions, García Bernal’s third directorial feature caters to the home side as a quasi-popular Mexican dramedy whose gags and in-jokes will play — if for anyone — more effectively to a Spanish-speaking crowd. 
	

	That’s not to make excuses, but to put in context, what is also a sputtering, screwball-y film about masculine roles in a waning patriarchal society. Get the script’s nuances or not, this awkwardly low-energy undertaking doesn’t make much of a case for García Bernal as a director, but as a star text in the mode of “Déficit,” his 2007 directorial debut, it’s got a fair bit to chew on by its own prismatic design. A TIFF slot will follow its premiere in Venice’s Spotlight section, and García Bernal’s profile is sure to fuel a healthy festival run. 


	Bits of narration from an offscreen speaker give the film a fairytale feel, a vibe matched by the rustic splendor of its chateau setting, where Camilo (García Bernal) lives with his athlete wife Jauna (Esmerelda Pimentel) and baby daughter. Camilo’s fortune, we learn from the opening address, came by a stroke of luck when he saved Juana’s businessman father Abel (Jorge Salinas) from drowning. Eternally grateful, Abel swiftly moved the Cuban lifeguard to Yucatán and placed him in a cushy corporate post at one of his companies. Jauna’s affections were secured shortly after — though apparently a jadedness has set into the marriage when the present timeline kicks off, and a rushed sex session devolves into a minor spat over who must tend to the crying babe. And does Juana even want to be touched by her husband? Facing the other direction, she asks him to make love to her with a different accent; to pretend that he’s another guy — maybe a Colombian dude. “From Cartagena or Bogota?” Camilo mutters. 
	

	“Hombre al Agua” then spins out into a game of shifting identities as a flurry of eccentric characters settle into the couple’s household. There’s Fabiana (Débora Nascimento), a statuesque Brazilian actress shadowing Jauna to prepare for a role as a pole-vaulter. Silvina (Natalia Oreiro), the Argentinian mistress and baby-momma of Abel, suspiciously begs Camilo to keep an eye on her while he recovers from a car accident. His daughter’s no-nonsense nanny, Malvina (Anna Diaz), side-eyes her bougie employers, while Silvina’s scruffy ex-husband, Ricardes (Manuel Garcia Rulfo), creeps around the gardens, occasionally drawing Camilo into a heart-to-heart. Meanwhile, at the factory Camilo manages for Abel, he’s a fumbling boss-man tasked with firing veteran workers and curbing their efforts to organize.

	The scenarios are vaguely zany, as when Fabiana Method-acts her way into Camilo’s bed, but the winding chattiness of the comedy is flatter than it is dry — like a bubbly beverage left too long uncapped. Pivots into a black-and-white Brazilian telenovela, which Camilo tunes into nightly while on baby duty, feed into the film’s nesting-doll narrative on paper, but in practice make for annoyingly gratuitous flourishes. In any case, the procession of masks, roles and stories (or versions of a story) that filter throughout make sense for what is ultimately an actor’s movie about the instability of a life lived as a series of parts. The web of characters make for a vaguely amusing assembly of nationalities, types and stereotypes, but insofar as they reflect back Camilo’s selves, that aspect is far too bleary and imprecise to build out a convincing personal crisis. 

	As the unravelling of a relationship, however, “Hombre al Agua” has a bit more going for it when Jauna decides to direct a movie about her own life, casting Fabiana (whom she may or may not be sleeping with) as herself and Robbie (Ricky Martin, making a brief stunt appearance) as a version of Camilo. Buried resentments come out through the script, and when Robbie unexpectedly drops the part, Camilo steps in to play himself, allowing for one of the film’s more arresting scenes, in which Jauna tenderly directs a sort of couple’s therapy between Camilo and Fabiana-as-Jauna. 
	

	It’s the peak for a movie that otherwise proceeds lifelessly though a few more unearned and perfunctory twists. Blowhard Abel, who is running for local office and wants Camilo as his right-hand man, turns out to be a Faustian figure whose influence must be denounced. Avenues for Camilo’s enlightenment while still remaining distinct and vivid personalities, the women impose change on García Bernal’s hapless hero, who might be the least interesting among them.

schema.headline: ‘Hombre al Agua’ Review: Gael García Bernal Directs and Stars in a Sputtering, Screwball-y Dramedy About One Man’s Identity Crisis

title: Robert Pattinson Is Having His Best Year Ever With ‘Primetime,’ ‘The Drama,’ ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Dune 3.’ Will the Oscars Recognize Him?
description:
Four Robert Pattinsons are better than one, and that makes his upcoming Oscar run a bit more complicated.

	In “Primetime,” Pattinson sits alone in
body:
Four Robert Pattinsons are better than one, and that makes his upcoming Oscar run a bit more complicated.

	In “Primetime,” Pattinson sits alone in a dim Florida room, reading a stranger’s chat logs aloud: “I will undress you as you undress me.” He’s playing Chris Hansen, host of the hidden-camera series “To Catch a Predator,” the man who turned police stings into television events that battled for ratings against the likes of ABC’s “Lost.” It’s the most uncomfortable thing Pattinson has ever done on screen (yet). It could also be what finally gets him an Oscar nomination.
	

	At 40, he’s yet to be recognized despite acclaimed turns in “Good Time,” “The Lighthouse” and “The Rover.” This year, Pattinson has stacked the deck.


	The evidence is all over the 2026 film year: indies, franchises and, in the middle of it all, shooting the next “Batman” movie with Matt Reeves.



	

									Courtesy of A24, Venice Film Festival
	



	In Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime,” which played in competition at Venice (earning a seven-minute standing ovation) and opens Sept. 25 through A24, Pattinson has what looks like his clearest awards vehicle. Kristoffer Borgli’s dark comedy “The Drama” gave him another showcase opposite Zendaya back in the spring. Then came Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” which became one of the year’s billion-dollar phenomena. And still to come, on Dec. 18, Denis Villeneuve’s final installment, “Dune: Part Three,” will give him a showier, villainous supporting turn as the shape-shifting Scytale.

	Four movies, two possible categories and two very different campaigns to juggle. Nobody’s asking anymore whether Pattinson belongs in the race. The question is how the studios — and Pattinson — choose to play it.
	

	“Primetime” seems to be the obvious one.

	Oppenheim, a documentarian who also helmed the Telluride surprise documentary “You Can See Everything” alongside Nathan Fielder, is making his narrative feature debut. His Hansen is a showman, the connective tissue of an anti-hero origin story à la “Joker” with Joaquin Phoenix and “American Psycho” with Christian Bale. The film isn’t out to canonize him. Instead, it watches everything that made him larger than the premise of the show: the ratings, the crew, the wannabe actors playing decoys and the audience who gobbled it up at home.

	Pattinson doesn’t ask anyone to root for Hansen, rather he asks them to sit with a man they’ve known from television and watch him squirm.

	We’ve seen a character get embraced like this before. Phoenix won lead actor for “Joker,” an ugly, uncomfortable character in a movie that split the room and still ran the table. “Primetime” operates in a similar space: loud enough to start a fight, familiar enough as an American story to give voters a way in.

	And Pattinson isn’t the only highlight.

	Skyler Gisondo, best known for roles in shows like HBO’s “The Righteous Gemstones” and most recently as Jimmy Olsen in James Gunn’s “Superman,” is terrific as Dan Plumb, the hopeful actor hired to play the bait. In many ways, he’s best in show. Also great alongside Gisondo is Emmy winner Merritt Wever (“Nurse Jackie”), who gives the producer an edge as the operation’s compromises pile up.

	And then there’s the real Hansen, who has been angling his way into the rollout with countless interviews and comments about the film. If nothing else, the movie now comes with a sideshow, and sideshows keep a title in the conversation. Look what Elon Musk did for “The Odyssey.”

	Unfortunately, Pattinson is a prime target for a vote-splitting scenario.

	He’s very good in Borgli’s comedy “The Drama” as a museum curator whose wedding quietly comes apart. In another year, it might have been the campaign. But it came out in April, and “Primetime” is the more recent entrant in the lead race.

	There’s also the fact that the lead actor race is incredibly competitive, with his “Odyssey” co-star Matt Damon in the thick of it, along with Andrew Scott (“Elsinore”), John Malkovich (“Wild Horse Nine”) and, still to come, Tom Cruise (“Digger”) and perhaps even his “Dune: Part Three” co-star Timothée Chalamet.
	

	The supporting race could be the leaner pathway.



	

									©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	In “The Odyssey,” Pattinson plays Antinous, ringleader of the suitors circling Penelope, and one piece of Nolan’s huge ensemble behind Damon’s Odysseus in what’s turning into one of the year’s biggest films. Best picture contenders of that size can float a supporting player, especially one the industry already respects. The question for Universal is whether the part is big enough, and sticky enough, to be worth the political capital. Could he split votes with his co-star John Leguizamo, or come along for the ride?

	“Dune: Part Three” is the other option, and potentially the showier one. Scytale is a bigger swing, Villeneuve is in his corner and Warner Bros. has a prime December date and real money in the franchise. The first two “Dune” films drew 15 Oscar nominations between them, so the Academy plainly takes the series seriously beyond the craft categories. But none of those nominations have been for acting.

	Either one could carry a real supporting push. But one wonders, could Pattinson actually land more than one nom?

	Jamie Foxx pulled it off in 2004, winning lead actor for “Ray” and landing a supporting nod for “Collateral.” Cate Blanchett did it in 2007, with a lead nomination for “Elizabeth: The Golden Age” and a supporting nomination for “I’m Not There.” The most recent was Scarlett Johansson in 2019, with “Marriage Story” and “Jojo Rabbit.” In addition, when you have a year of multiple titles, the Academy looks for the “representation”-type of film like they did with Jessica Chastain (nominated for “The Help” in a seven-film year) and Philip Seymour Hoffman (nominated for “Charlie Wilson’s War” in supporting actor, with two lead acclaimed works in “Before the Devil Knows You’re Dead” and “The Savages”).

	And let’s not forget, actors can now be double-nominated in the same category following an Academy rule update earlier this year.

	That’s no guarantee for any of this. “Primetime” might play too harshly for a chunk of the Academy, while “The Odyssey” and “Dune: Part Three” could be technical players with other actors to be recognized.

	Nonetheless, Pattinson stopped having us ask the question if he was a great actor a while ago. What’s left is for the Academy, and its four Pattinsons before them, to talk themselves into checking the right box.

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson Is Having His Best Year Ever With ‘Primetime,’ ‘The Drama,’ ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Dune 3.’ Will the Oscars Recognize Him?

title: NJ Hairdresser Charged After Allegedly Hiring Tinder Hitman to Kill Ex-BF
description:
New Jersey Hairdresser
                          Fed Say She Hired Hitman to Kill Ex-BF
body:
New Jersey Hairdresser
                          Fed Say She Hired Hitman to Kill Ex-BF
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 11, 2026
                            9:21 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A New Jersey woman just got busted in an alleged murder-for-hire plot ... federal prosecutors say she paid a man she met on Tinder money to whack her ex-boyfriend -- a police officer -- and his teenage daughter.
      
    
            According to the Department of Justice, Jaclyn Diiorio -- a 28-year-old from Runnemede, NJ -- has been charged with two counts of using interstate commerce facilities in an attempt to commission a murder-for-hire.
      
    
            The feds claim Diiorio tried to use her cell phone to pay for the murders of Matthew O'Hanlon -- a Philadelphia police officer -- and his 19-year-old daughter.
      

            Diiorio allegedly met a fake hitman -- who cops say is a confidential informant -- on the popular dating app ... and authorities say they exchanged multiple phone calls in late March/early April 2025 during which they allegedly organized the hits.
      
    
            Feds say Diiorio met with the informant at a Dollar General on April 4 and allegedly gave him $500 as a down payment and promised to pay an additional $12,000 in installments.
      
    
            The C.I. then called local cops and reported Diiorio's alleged misdeeds. She was arrested by Camden County officers and charged with two counts of first-degree attempted murder, one count of first-degree conspiracy to commit murder, and one count of third-degree possession of a controlled dangerous substance ... though the state dismissed her charges after the federal indictment was handed down.
      
    
            Diiorio's attorney, Robert Gamburg, told the Philadelphia Inquirer his client will plead not guilty. She has a court hearing scheduled for Monday.

            A 5th plane was targeted by terrorists on 9/11 -- something the government does not want you to know -- so says the pilot, the flight attendants, the airline's dispatcher, and others.
      
    
            TMZ produced a documentary -- "TMZ Investigates 9/11: The Fifth Plane" -- which is currently on YouTube. The doc described the events on United Flight 23, which was scheduled to take off from JFK at 9:00 AM, with Los Angeles as the final destination.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            There were 7 people who raised suspicion on the part of the crew, checking out the cockpit, arguing with a flight attendant not to delay the takeoff over a food issue.
      

            There's hard evidence people were hiding in the hatch of the plane ... only to surface after the plane was evacuated and locked ... presumably looking to recover incriminating evidence.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The FBI secretly interviewed the entire flight crew, and even presented them with a lineup.
      
    
            Yet Flight 23 became a deep, dark secret ... the government, the FBI, and United Airlines have all been radio silent.
